name: Aristocrat Records
description: Aristocrat Records was a Chicago record label founded in April 1947 by Charles and Evelyn Aron with partners Fred and Mildred Brount and Art Spiegel, working in blues and jazz. Leonard Chess invested in the young company that September and steadily bought the other partners out, so that by 1948 only he and Evelyn Aron ran the firm. In early 1950 Leonard and his brother Phil Chess became the sole owners, and in June 1950 they renamed the company Chess Records; the Aristocrat brand itself was officially discontinued in January 1951. In its three years Aristocrat released 183 songs and recorded eighteen more that later appeared under the Chess name. Its most consequential signing was Muddy Waters, who made his first Aristocrat recordings on August 27, 1947. A second session that December produced the single pairing his versions of two traditional songs, which became a minor hit and pointed the label — and soon Chess — toward the down-home electric blues that would define Chicago's sound. Aristocrat is therefore staged as the direct predecessor institution to the graph's homed Chess Records (CTL-E-0165).

name: Abiodun Oyewole
description: Abiodun Oyewole (born Charles Davis, February 25, 1948, Cincinnati, Ohio) is a poet, teacher, and founding member of the spoken-word group the Last Poets. Raised in Queens, New York, amid jazz and gospel records and the poetry of Langston Hughes, he received his Yoruba name at fifteen at a temple in Harlem. On May 19, 1968 — Malcolm X's birthday — Oyewole, David Nelson, and Gylan Kain performed at a Malcolm X memorial in Harlem, and the Last Poets were born; their percussive, Black-nationalist poetry, first recorded in 1970, is widely credited with laying groundwork for hip-hop. A prison term in North Carolina interrupted his tenure; on study release he earned a bachelor's degree, later completing a doctorate at Columbia University, where he served on the faculty. He rejoined the group for its 1990s resurgence and continues to write, publish, perform, and host a weekly artists' salon at his Harlem home.

name: Alain Locke
aliases: Alain LeRoy Locke; Dean of the Harlem Renaissance (epithet)
description: Alain LeRoy Locke (1885–1954) was the philosopher who named and framed the Harlem Renaissance. Born in Philadelphia, he graduated from Harvard in 1907 and became the first African American Rhodes Scholar, studying at Oxford and Berlin before completing a Harvard PhD in philosophy in 1918. Locke spent his teaching career at Howard University (1912–1953), where he built one of the first philosophy departments at a historically Black college and developed a philosophy of race as social and cultural inheritance rather than biology, joined to theories of value pluralism and cultural relativism. In March 1925 he edited the Survey Graphic issue “Harlem, Mecca of the New Negro” and expanded it into The New Negro: An Interpretation, the anthology of fiction, poetry, essays, and art — Hughes, Hurston, Cullen, Toomer, and others — that announced the Renaissance to the nation and earned him the title of its Dean. A tireless advocate for Black art, he wrote Negro Art: Past and Present (1936) and The Negro in Art (1940), edited the Bronze Booklet series in the 1930s, and in 1941 organized the first commercial exhibition of African American art in New York. He retired from Howard in 1953 and died the following year.

name: Amelia Boynton Robinson
aliases: Amelia Boynton; Amelia Platts Boynton Robinson
description: Amelia Boynton Robinson, born Amelia Platts on 18 August 1911 in Savannah, Georgia, was a leading organizer of the Selma voting-rights campaign. Educated at Georgia State College and Tuskegee Institute, where she earned a home economics degree in 1927, she came to Selma as the U.S. Department of Agriculture's home demonstration agent for Dallas County. With her husband, Samuel Boynton, she spent decades registering Black voters and bringing federal programs to rural families. In 1964 she became the first African American woman in Alabama to run for Congress. She invited Martin Luther King Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference to Selma, opened her office and home to the movement, and helped plan the 1965 marches. On Bloody Sunday, 7 March 1965, state troopers beat her unconscious on the Edmund Pettus Bridge; a photograph of her crumpled figure carried the Selma story worldwide, and she marched in the completed Selma to Montgomery march later that month. She received the Martin Luther King Jr. Freedom Medal in 1990. In March 2015 she crossed the Pettus Bridge hand in hand with President Barack Obama for the fiftieth anniversary. She died in Montgomery on 26 August 2015, aged 104.

name: Ayo Edebiri
description: Ayo Edebiri, born 3 October 1995 in Boston, Massachusetts, is an American actress, comedian and writer. She was raised in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood in a Pentecostal household by immigrant parents — her father from Nigeria and her mother from Barbados — and found comedy through drama class and the improv club at Boston Latin School. At New York University she switched from teaching to dramatic writing, graduating in 2017, and built a career in New York stand-up and television writing, joining Big Mouth as a writer and, from 2020, the voice of Missy. Her breakthrough came as sous chef Sydney Adamu in the FX series The Bear (2022– ), a performance that won her a Primetime Emmy Award, a Golden Globe Award and a Screen Actors Guild Award; she has also directed an episode of the series, 'Napkins,' earning a directing nomination. Her film work includes Theater Camp and Bottoms (2023) and voice roles in Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (2023) and Inside Out 2 (2024).

name: Andre Rush
description: Andre Rush, born 7 September 1974 in Columbus, Mississippi, is an American chef and retired United States Army master sergeant. He enlisted in the Army in 1993 and served twenty-four years, cooking as a member of the United States Culinary Arts Team and as senior enlisted aide at West Point, and he began cooking at the White House in 1997, working part-time across the administrations of Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Donald Trump while also serving at the Pentagon, where he was present on 11 September 2001 and afterwards volunteered for combat duties. A photograph of him preparing the White House Iftar dinner in June 2018 made his 24-inch biceps a national story; he is known for performing 2,222 push-ups a day to raise awareness of veteran suicide. After leaving the White House kitchen he moved into television, starring in the restaurant-rescue series Kitchen Commando on Tubi in 2023, and he remains a fixture of Army public life, photographed doing push-ups with soldiers at the Army's 250th birthday festival on the National Mall in June 2025 and visiting soldiers in South Korea that December.

name: Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor
description: Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor is an American actress born on February 21, 1969, in San Francisco, California, and raised on her grandmother's farm in Magnolia, Mississippi. She attended Tougaloo College before transferring to Brown University, where she completed a B.A. in African American studies, and she studied acting in the Graduate Acting Program at New York University's Tisch School of the Arts. She made her professional acting debut in 1995 opposite Patrick Stewart in a Broadway revival of The Tempest. Her screen work includes Men of Honor, Ray, The Help, The Birth of a Nation, and If Beale Street Could Talk, and acclaimed television roles in When They See Us and Lovecraft Country, each bringing Primetime Emmy Award nominations. For her portrayal of Oracene Price in King Richard in 2021 she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. She has since starred in Origin in 2023 as Isabel Wilkerson and in Nickel Boys in 2024. In 2023 she began using the double-barrelled professional name Ellis-Taylor in honor of her mother.

name: Alfreda Barnett Duster
aliases: Alfreda M. Barnett Duster; Alfreda Barnett
description: Alfreda Barnett Duster, born Alfreda Barnett on September 3, 1904, in Chicago, was the youngest daughter of civil rights leaders Ida B. Wells and Ferdinand L. Barnett. She graduated from the University of Chicago in 1924 with a bachelor of philosophy degree, married Benjamin C. Duster Jr., and raised five children; widowed at forty, she returned to school for social work. As a Chicago social worker and civic leader she served as a juvenile delinquency prevention coordinator for the State of Illinois, assigned to the Southside Community Committee, administered the girls' program at Camp Illini for underprivileged city children, and later worked for the Woodlawn Community Services Agency and Catalyst for Youth. She was named Mother of the Year in 1950 and 1970 and received a University of Chicago Alumni Association Citation for Public Service and an honorary doctorate from Chicago State University. Her enduring editorial achievement was editing and publishing her mother's autobiography as Crusade for Justice: The Autobiography of Ida B. Wells (University of Chicago Press, 1970), work the sources say she pursued for twenty-five years after her mother's death. She died April 2, 1983, in Chicago, aged seventy-eight.

name: Ainsley Harriott
description: Ainsley Denzil Dubriel Harriott, born 28 February 1957 in Paddington, London, is an English chef, television presenter and author of Jamaican heritage. The son of Chester Harriott, a Jamaican-born pianist and singer, he trained at Westminster Kingsway College, worked in West End kitchens and became head chef of the Long Room at Lord's Cricket Ground, while performing in the comedy-music duo the Calypso Twins. Television made him one of Britain's most recognisable cooks: resident chef on Good Morning with Anne and Nick, then presenter of Can't Cook, Won't Cook and, from 2000 to 2010, Ready Steady Cook, whose twenty-one series fixed his exuberant style in the national memory. His cookbooks have sold more than two million copies worldwide. He has spoken publicly about being refused head-chef jobs in his early career explicitly because he was Black. Appointed MBE in the 2020 New Year Honours for services to broadcasting and the culinary arts, he continues to front ITV food series including Ainsley's Fantastic Flavours, and was still making festival and store appearances in the summer of 2026.

name: Asia Monet Ray
description: Asia Monet Ray, born 10 August 2005 in Yorba Linda, California, is an American dancer, singer and actress, now performing as Asia Monét. The daughter of former professional bodybuilder Shawn Ray, who is African American, and Kristie Ray, she began dancing at two. She finished third in the first season of Abby's Ultimate Dance Competition in 2012 and joined Lifetime's Dance Moms for its third season in 2013. In 2014 Lifetime gave her family their own series, Raising Asia, and she released her self-titled debut recording. She played Sydney Simpson, the daughter of O. J. Simpson, in FX's The People v. O. J. Simpson: American Crime Story in 2016 and also appeared on Grey's Anatomy. She graduated from high school in 2023. As an adult she has worked as an independent recording artist; in 2026 she discussed her new era of music and her upcoming single in a Spout Podcast interview, and sang the national anthem at the Olympia in September 2026.

name: Adriana Lima
description: Adriana Lima, born 12 June 1981 in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, is a Brazilian model. Raised in Salvador's Castelo Branco neighbourhood by her mother, Maria das Graças Lima, a social worker, she won Ford's Supermodel of Brazil search at fifteen and placed second in the Ford Models Supermodel of the World contest in 1996, then moved to New York and signed with Elite Model Management. She made her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in 1999 and was a Victoria's Secret Angel from 2000 to 2018, the longest-running Angel in the brand's history, opening the show five times and wearing the Fantasy Bra three times. Named the most valuable Victoria's Secret Angel by D'Marie in 2017, she was a Maybelline spokesmodel and an ambassador for Desigual, Calzedonia, IWC, Puma and Chopard. In 2023 FIFA named her its first Global Fan Ambassador. She was confirmed in September 2026 for the Victoria's Secret 2026 Fashion Show.

name: Anok Yai
description: Anok Yai, born 20 December 1997 in Cairo, Egypt, is an American fashion model of South Sudanese descent. Born after her family fled genocide in Sudan, she moved at age three to Manchester, New Hampshire, graduated from Manchester High School West and studied biochemistry at Plymouth State University, intending to become a doctor. A photograph taken at Howard University's homecoming in October 2017 went viral, leading her to sign with Next Model Management. In February 2018 she opened the Prada show, becoming the first South Sudanese model to open for the house and the second Black model to do so, after Naomi Campbell in 1997. She has since walked and fronted campaigns for Versace, Louis Vuitton, Fendi, Burberry and Mugler, appeared on multiple international Vogue covers including American Vogue three times, was named Models.com Model of the Year in 2023 and Model of the Year by the British Fashion Council in December 2025, and was named one of TIME's 100 most influential people in 2026.

name: Ayesha Curry
description: Ayesha Curry, born Ayesha Disa Alexander on 23 March 1989 in Ontario, Canada, is a Canadian-American businessperson, cookbook author and television host. Raised in Markham, Ontario, until she was fourteen, when her family moved to Charlotte, North Carolina, she first pursued acting, with guest roles from 2008 including an appearance on Hannah Montana. After marrying basketball player Stephen Curry in 2011, she built a food career from her Little Lights of Mine blog and YouTube channel, launched in 2014. Her Food Network series Ayesha's Homemade, later Ayesha's Home Kitchen, began in 2016, and she has published two cookbooks, The Seasoned Life (2016) and The Full Plate (2020). She is the founder and chief executive of Sweet July, a lifestyle brand launched in 2020 that celebrates women and BIPOC creators, and a co-founder of the Domaine Curry wine brand. In February 2026 she attended the Los Angeles premiere of GOAT, the animated film she made with her husband.

name: Afro-American Council
description: The Afro-American Council was established in Rochester, New York, in September 1898 by newspaper editor T. Thomas Fortune and Bishop Alexander Walters of the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, as a revival of the earlier National Afro-American League. The immediate impetus was the murder of African American postmaster Frazier B. Baker in Lake City, South Carolina, by a white mob. Bishop Walters served as its first president, with Ida B. Wells of Chicago as secretary and John C. Dancy of North Carolina as vice president, and its membership drew journalists, attorneys, educators, politicians and community activists, including Mary Church Terrell, W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington. The Council opposed lynching, the disfranchisement of Black voters and racial discrimination, lobbied for a federal anti-lynching law, and welcomed women as equal members, among the first Black organizations to do so. It met regularly with President William McKinley between 1898 and 1901. Torn by pro- and anti-Washington factionalism, it held its final meeting in Baltimore in 1907, but it helped train activists who went on to create the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People in 1909.

name: Amber Ruffin
description: Amber Ruffin (born January 9, 1979, in Omaha, Nebraska) is an American comedian, writer, actress, and playwright whose hiring changed late-night television. Trained in improvisation, she performed in Omaha, moved through Chicago's iO Theater and The Second City, and worked with Boom Chicago in Amsterdam before joining the writing staff of Late Night with Seth Meyers at its 2014 launch. Industry and magazine sources agree on the significance of that appointment: she was the first Black woman to write for a late-night network talk show in the United States. She also performs on the program in recurring segments. From 2020 she hosted her own topical late-night program, The Amber Ruffin Show, on NBCUniversal's Peacock service; sources differ slightly on its run, with Out magazine giving 2020 to 2023 and her encyclopedia entry giving 2020 to 2022 for the Peacock run. With her sister Lacey Lamar she co-authored the New York Times best-selling book published in January 2021 and a second book in 2022, and she co-wrote the book for the Broadway musical adaptation of Some Like It Hot. In 2025 she was continuing on CNN's Have I Got News for You and developing new stage work, remaining an active public performer.

name: AOL BlackVoices
aliases: BlackVoices.com; Black Voices; HuffPost Black Voices; AOL Black Voices
description: AOL Black Voices was an American website and online community serving African American audiences, launched in 1995 as BlackVoices.com. It was developed by editor Barry Cooper as part of Tribune-owned Orlando Sentinel Online, with its first home on America Online, and was later spun off into its own website. In February 2004 AOL acquired the site from Tribune Co. after months of negotiations; InternetNews reported it as an 883,000-member website and one of the country's largest African American websites, joining an AOL umbrella that already included a Black Focus channel and Africana.com. Under AOL the property operated as AOL Black Voices, with news and entertainment content aimed at African American readers and a strongly engaged member community. In March 2011 it ranked third among Black-oriented websites in comScore figures reported by Journal-isms, behind MediaTakeOut.com and BET.com. That same month AOL acquired The Huffington Post, and Black Voices came under Huffington Post control; the planned new GlobalBlack site was scrapped in favor of reshaping Black Voices, which continued as HuffPost Black Voices, a section of HuffPost. The standalone AOL-era property was thus transformed rather than simply closed: the brand and audience carried into HuffPost, while its independent site identity ended.

name: Adam Clayton Powell Jr.
description: Adam Clayton Powell Jr. was a Baptist pastor and Democratic congressman who represented Harlem in the U.S. House of Representatives. Born in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1908 and raised in New York, he graduated from Colgate University in 1930 and earned a master's degree from Columbia University in 1932. He served Abyssinian Baptist Church as manager and assistant pastor from 1930 and succeeded his father as pastor in 1937, holding that pulpit until 1971. Elected to the New York City Council in 1941, he founded and edited the People's Voice newspaper in 1942 and entered Congress in 1945 as the first Black congressman from the northeastern United States. From 1961 he chaired the House Committee on Education and Labor. The House excluded him in March 1967; voters reelected him, he was seated again in 1969 after the Supreme Court ruled the exclusion unconstitutional, and he lost renomination in 1970.

name: African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund
description: The African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund is a preservation program of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, launched in November 2017 to protect places tied to African American activism, achievement, and resilience. The National Trust describes it as the largest preservation effort ever undertaken in support of African American historic sites and, at launch, as a $25 million campaign and the largest fundraising and historic preservation campaign on behalf of Black history by a private nonprofit. Led at launch by executive director Brent Leggs, the fund works with communities and grassroots stewards, invests in and restores cultural assets, and runs a national grant program intended to fund projects, advance their missions, and bring national attention to Black historic places that have too often gone unrecognized in the American landscape.

name: Alexander Crummell
description: Alexander Crummell was a nineteenth-century Episcopal priest, missionary, scholar, and teacher born in New York City in 1819 to free Black parents. Denied admission to the Episcopal Church's General Theological Seminary because of his race, he studied privately and became an Episcopal minister at twenty-five; diocesan records place his ordination to the diaconate in 1842 and to the priesthood in 1844. From 1848 to 1853 he lectured and studied in England, graduating from Queens' College, Cambridge, in 1853, then took a faculty position at Liberia College in Monrovia and urged African American emigration to Liberia. Internal politics forced him to leave Liberia in 1872. Returning to Washington, D.C., he founded St. Luke's Episcopal Church, helped organize opposition to a segregated missionary district, taught at Howard University from 1895 to 1897, and in 1897 helped found the American Negro Academy as its first president.

name: All Platinum Records
description: All Platinum Records was an Englewood, New Jersey, soul and R&B label started in 1967 by singer, writer, and producer Sylvia Robinson and her husband, businessman Joe Robinson. Working from the company's own Soul Sound Studios with in-house musicians, Sylvia Robinson ran the creative operation and produced or co-produced many releases, while subsidiary labels included Stang, Vibration, Turbo, and Astroscope. The label's mainstay act was The Moments, who stayed for ten years and scored a million-selling hit in 1970 that reached number one on the R&B chart and number three on the pop chart. Other number-one R&B hits for the group of labels included Sylvia's own solo hit in 1973 and Shirley & Company's hit in 1975. In 1975 the company bought the bankrupt Chess Records with PolyGram assistance, an unsuccessful move, and in 1979 the Robinsons launched Sugar Hill Records as its focus shifted to rap.

name: Arthur Ashe
description: Arthur Ashe was an American tennis champion and civil-rights activist born in Richmond, Virginia, on July 10, 1943. Raised under segregation, he began playing at age seven, was coached by Walter Johnson and Richard Hudlin, and attended the University of California, Los Angeles, on a tennis scholarship, winning intercollegiate singles and doubles titles in 1965. In 1963 he became the first Black member of the U.S. Davis Cup team. In 1968 he won the first U.S. Open of the modern open era, becoming the first Black player to win a major men's singles championship; he added the Australian Open in 1970 and Wimbledon in 1975, beating the heavily favored Jimmy Connors, and remains the only Black man to have won the men's singles title at those events. A co-founder of the Association of Tennis Professionals in 1972, he retired in 1980, captained the Davis Cup team from 1981 to 1985, campaigned against South African apartheid, and after revealing in April 1992 that he had AIDS, devoted his final months to educating the public about the disease. He died in New York on February 6, 1993.

name: Auburn Avenue
aliases: Sweet Auburn; Sweet Auburn Historic District; Wheat Street (former name)
description: Auburn Avenue, known as Sweet Auburn, is Atlanta's historic Black commercial corridor, running less than two miles eastward from Peachtree Street. Renamed from Wheat Street in 1893, the avenue rose to prominence as Jim Crow laws confined Black Atlantans to the city's east side, and it became the commercial, cultural, and spiritual center of Black Atlanta. Its financial anchors included Alonzo Herndon's Atlanta Life Insurance Company, founded in 1905, and Citizens Trust Bank, and the street held Ebenezer Baptist Church and Big Bethel AME Church, the Atlanta Daily World, and clubs such as the Top Hat, later the Royal Peacock. Civic leader John Wesley Dobbs coined the name Sweet Auburn, and in 1956 Fortune described the avenue in the period's wording as the richest Negro street in the world. Martin Luther King Jr. was born at 501 Auburn Avenue. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1976, the district declined with integration-era disinvestment and the Downtown Connector's construction, and preservation efforts continue.

name: Avery Wilson
description: Avery Wilson is an American R&B singer, songwriter, dancer and actor from Hamden, Connecticut. Born Branden Avery Wilson on July 18, 1995, he was nine when his father — who oversaw fourteen area McDonald's restaurants as a director of operations — began staging open-mic nights at one of them so the boy could perform; Wilson still returns to help with the event. His demo "Ringtone" won regional radio airplay across Connecticut, New York and Massachusetts, and songwriter-producer Sean Garrett began developing him; in 2011 he co-won New York's Next Teen Superstar competition. In 2012 he self-released On Top of the World and, at sixteen, reached the knockout rounds of The Voice's third season on Team Cee Lo Green — an elimination Rolling Stone covered as an upset. Signed to Clive Davis and RCA Records, he released his first official single, "If I Have To," in May 2015; it peaked at No. 18 on Billboard's Hot R&B Songs chart. After further RCA singles, among them "Change My Mind" featuring Migos, he went independent with the EPs FYI (2018) and 8:34 (2019). In 2024 he starred as the Scarecrow in the Broadway revival of The Wiz, and as a principal vocalist on its cast recording he earned his first Grammy nomination, for Best Musical Theater Album at the 67th Grammy Awards. In June 2026 he sang the national anthem throughout the New York Knicks' championship playoff run — including Game 3 of the NBA Finals — and performed at the team's City Hall championship ceremony.

name: Aaron Mallory
description: Aaron Mallory is the founder and CEO of GRO Community, a Chicago-based nonprofit delivering culturally grounded, trauma-informed mental health and social services for boys and men of color, including therapy, workforce supports and reentry services. A licensed clinical social worker in Illinois, he holds an MSW from the University of Chicago and previously held direct-service and leadership roles at UCAN and Heartland Alliance, where he was Clinical Director of the READI initiative; his professional biography credits him with more than ten years in the field. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Aaron Smoot
description: Aaron Smoot is Community Engagement & Advancement Manager at The CAFE Group (the Cleveland Avenue Foundation for Education), a Chicago-founded national nonprofit established in 2014 by Don and Liz Thompson that supports students and education leaders of color; its 1954 Project awards $1 million grants to Black-led education nonprofits. Smoot was named a Surge Fellowship Chicago 2027 Fellow under that title. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Alexa Rice
description: Alexa Rice is the founder of Beech Beauty, a Chicago beauty company launched with a line of high-shine lip glosses, a portion of whose proceeds funds tree planting in underserved urban communities. Coverage in JWC Media and AfroTech (reporting WBEZ Chicago) identifies her as a granddaughter of John H. and Eunice Johnson, founders of Johnson Publishing Company (Ebony and Jet) and Fashion Fair, and reports that she developed the brand during the final year of her master's program at Harvard Divinity School. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Allen C. Shelton
description: Allen C. Shelton is co-founder and Chief Creative Officer of Narratent Digital Marketing, a Chicago digital marketing and branding agency whose partnerships have included NBC Sports, BET Media Group and Universal Music Group; he leads the agency alongside CEO and co-founder Desmon Walker, a fellow Southern Illinois University graduate. WVON's roster credits him in the shortened form 'Founder & CCO.' He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Ariel D. Rainey
description: Ariel D. Rainey — spelled Ariel DeNey Rainey in Obama Foundation and organizational sources — is the founder and CEO of Hustle Mommies, a Chicago nonprofit that equips urban and Black mothers to lead in business, policy and community through trauma-informed advocacy, economic empowerment and entrepreneurship. The Obama Foundation named her a 2025–2026 USA Leader, crediting her with mobilizing more than 3,500 mothers, helping secure over $125,000 in startup funding for Black mom-owned businesses, and founding the 'Paint the Hood Orange' gun-violence initiative. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Aris Singleton
description: Aris Singleton is CEO of Thank God It's Natural (tgin), the Black-owned textured hair and skincare brand founded in 2009 by her aunt, Chris-Tia Donaldson, and sold at Target, Walmart, Ulta Beauty, Sally Beauty, Walgreens and CVS. Singleton, who holds a BA in Finance from Texas Southern University, returned to the company in 2017 and became CEO following Donaldson's death in November 2021. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Ashlee Feemster
description: Ashlee Feemster is a Director at BET (Black Entertainment Television) in Chicago, credited on WVON's Class of 2026 roster as Director, Brand Solutions. The Chicago Advertising Federation's membership directory lists her as Director, Integrated Marketing at BET, and professional-profile data places her in BET's Brand Solutions function in the Greater Chicago Area at manager level before the rostered directorship; the roster's exact title wording is not independently confirmed. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Ashley Coleman
description: Ashley Coleman is President of C&G Construction Supply Company, a Calumet City, Illinois construction-supply firm the company describes as 100% minority- and women-owned, certified at city, county, state and national levels and founded in 2009. Her presidency is documented on WVON's Class of 2026 roster; no independent source naming her was located in this pass. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
